about.title: Jurupa Valley Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Jurupa Valley's mix of logistics, distribution, and industrial work along corridors like Limonite Avenue and Mission Boulevard means workplace injuries here often involve heavy equipment, forklifts, delivery vehicles, or repetitive strain. In most cases, California workers' compensation is the only path against your own employer, no matter who was at fault. But when a subcontractor, equipment manufacturer, property owner, or another driver contributed to your injury, a separate third-party claim may also be possible. Sorting out which applies — and whether both apply at once — can be confusing, especially while you're recovering and dealing with medical bills. LawProactive doesn't practice law; we simply connect injured workers in Riverside County with an independent attorney who can look at the details of your situation and explain your options, free of charge and with no obligation.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney About a Workplace Injury

items.title: Workers' Comp Isn't Always the Whole Picture
items.desc: While workers' compensation is usually your exclusive remedy against your employer, a negligent third party — like a subcontractor or equipment maker — may still be separately liable. An attorney can help identify if that applies to your case.

items.title: Reporting Deadlines Matter
items.desc: California generally requires you to report a workplace injury to your employer within 30 days. Missing that window can complicate your claim, so getting guidance early matters.

items.title: Retaliation Is Against the Law
items.desc: Employers cannot legally punish you for reporting an injury or filing a workers' comp claim. If you're worried about your job, an independent attorney can explain your protections.

items.question: I was hurt on a job site near Mission Boulevard — can I still file a claim if it wasn't entirely my employer's fault?
items.answer: Workers' compensation generally applies regardless of fault when it comes to your employer. But if another party, like a contractor or equipment supplier, contributed to your injury, that may open the door to a separate third-party claim. An attorney can look at the specifics and let you know what applies.

items.question: What's the deadline to report a workplace injury in California?
items.answer: You generally need to notify your employer within 30 days of the injury to protect your workers' comp rights. If a third-party claim is also involved, that carries a separate 2-year deadline. Acting sooner rather than later helps preserve your options.

items.question: Can my employer fire me for reporting an injury?
items.answer: No — retaliation against an employee for reporting a workplace injury or filing a workers' comp claim is illegal in California. If you're facing pressure at work after an injury, it's worth speaking with an independent attorney about your rights.
